topics.title: Our Weather - Meaning of Weather Symbols | Weather Records and Charts Primary 4 (Basic 4) and Primary 6 (Basic 6) - Basic Science and Technology ASEI PDSI METHOD
topics.content:
BASIC SCIENCE (BST)
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
SMASE - ASEI PDSI METHOD
FIRST TERM
WEEK 6/PRIMARY 4
WEEK 4/PRIMARY 6
THEME - LEARNING ABOUT OUR ENVIRONMENT
PREVIOUS LESSON - Meaning of Weather and Factors Affecting the Weather (Primary 4) ASEI PDSI METHOD
TOPIC - OUR WEATHER
LEARNING AREA
Lesson One - Meaning and Symbols of Weather
Lesson Two - Weather Records and Chart
Lesson Three - Revision and Test
TIME - 40 Minutes each.
LEARNING OUTCOME
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. identify and write simple weather symbols;
2. observe weather changes over a period of about three weeks;
3. use the weather symbols to keep records of weather changes;
4. prepare a weather chart.
RATIONALE
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular time. The following are weather symbols sunny, cloudy, cloudy with sunshine, sunny with rainfall, cloudy with thunder, etc. representing the the sun, the rainfall, the cloud, the wind, etc.
Weather symbols are used internationally to communicate the weather forecast to people. The value of using a symbol is that it contains no words and can therefore be easy to understand.
The concept of weather, symbols and charts will enable the pupils to understand and records weather of the day using appropriate symbols.
LEARNING MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
Weather symbols
Weather chart
Cardboard
Writing materials
PREVIOUS KNOWLEDGE
The pupils can tell when it cloudy and about to rain. They are aware of different things that comes along with the rain - storm  thunder, wind, dust, etc. After rainy season comes the dry season, sunny days.

Basic Science and Technology

topics.content:
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY - 50 MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS (MCQs) WITH ANSWER KEY FOR PRIMARY 6
INSTRUCTION - Choose the correct answer from the options A - D.
1. Air is a mixture of _____. A. liquids only B. solids C. water D. gases
2. The gas needed for breathing is _____. A. nitrogen B. oxygen C. carbon dioxide D. hydrogen
3. Moving air is called _____. A. breeze B. storm C. wind D. cloud
4. Which of these shows that air occupies space? A. Air has colour B. Inflated balloon C. Air has taste D. Air has sound
5. Climate change means _____. A. daily weather changes B. rainfall only C. hot afternoons D. long-term change in weather conditions
6. One cause of climate change is _____. A. tree planting B. deforestation C. recycling D. rainfall
7. Burning fossil fuels releases _____. A. oxygen B. nitrogen C. carbon dioxide D. hydrogen
8. One effect of climate change is _____. A. stable seasons B. flooding C. fresh air D. planting trees
9. The Earth rotates on its _____. A. orbit B. surface C. moon D. axis
10. One complete rotation of the Earth causes _____. A. a year B. a month C. day and night D. seasons
11. The movement of the Earth around the sun is called _____. A. Revolution B. rotation C. vibration D. motion
12. One complete revolution of the Earth takes _____. A. 24 hours B. 7 days C. 30 days D. 365 days
13. The solar system has _____ at the center. A. the moon B. Earth C. the sun D. Mars
14. Which of these is NOT a planet? A. Earth B. Moon C. Venus D. Mars
15. The planet closest to the sun is _____. A. Earth B. Venus C. Mercury D. Mars
16. The largest planet in the solar system is _____. A. Earth B. Jupiter C. Saturn D. Uranus
17. Colours seen when sunlight passes through rain are called _____. A. shadow B. spectrum C. reflection D. mirror
18. The three primary colours are _____. A. red, blue, yellow B. green, orange, purple C. black, white, grey D. pink, brown, gold
19. Mixing red and blue gives _____. A. green B. yellow C. purple D. orange
20. White colour reflects _____. A. no light B. some light C. red light D. all light
21. The smallest particle of an element is called _____. A. molecule B. cell C. Compound D. atom
22. An element is a substance that _____. A. contains many compounds B. cannot be broken into simpler substances C. is always liquid D. has colour
23. Oxygen is an example of _____. A. element B. compound C. mixture D. solution
24. Elements are arranged in the _____. A. timetable B. register C. periodic table D. notebook
25. Woodwork is the art of working with _____. A. metal B. plastic C. wood D. glass
26. A saw is used for _____. A. painting B. cutting wood C. measuring D. drilling
27. A hammer is used for _____. A. pulling nails B. cutting wood C. fixing nails D. sanding wood
28. A tape rule is used for _____. A. measuring B. cutting C. nailing D. shaping
29. Maintenance means _____. A. destroying tools B. repairing and caring for tools C. hiding tools D. selling tools
30. One reason for maintaining tools is to _____. A. spoil them B. lose them C. rust them D. make them last longer
31. Oiling metal tools helps to prevent _____. A. cutting B. rusting C. breaking D. bending
32. Tools should be stored in a _____. A. classroom B. cupboard or toolbox C. playground D. dustbin
33. Safety means _____. A. freedom from danger B. playing carelessly C. running everywhere D. breaking rules
34. Wearing goggles in the workshop helps to protect the _____. A. hands B. feet C. eyes D. ears
35. One safety rule in the workshop is to _____. A. run around B. misuse tools C. follow instructions D. joke with tools
36. Sharp tools should be handled _____. A. carelessly B. playfully C. carefully D. wrongly
37. Carbon dioxide is useful to plants for _____. A. breathing B. photosynthesis C. sleeping D. eating
38. Flooding can be reduced by _____. A. cutting trees B. planting trees C. burning bushes D. blocking drainage
39. The Earth gets light from the _____. A. moon B. stars C. sun D. clouds
40. The moon is a _____. A. planet B. star C. satellite D. comet
41. Mixing yellow and blue gives _____. A. orange B. green C. purple D. brown
42. Hydrogen is an example of _____. A. element B. mixture C. Compound D. solution
43. A chisel is mainly used in woodwork for _____. A. measuring B. cutting and shaping wood C. painting D. joining papers
44. Cleaning tools after use is an example of _____. A. misuse B. maintenance C. waste D. danger
45. Wearing gloves helps to protect the _____. A. hands B. eyes C. head D. legs
46. One effect of air pollution is _____. A. fresh air B. good health C. breathing problems D. clean sky
47. The layer of air around the Earth is called _____. A. hydrosphere B. atmosphere C. lithosphere D. biosphere
48. The sun is a _____. A. planet B. satellite C. asteroid D. star
49. A screwdriver is used to _____. A. cut wood B. tighten or loosen screws C. measure wood D. paint surfaces
50. Obeying safety rules helps to prevent _____. A. learning B. success C. fun D. accidents

topics.title: Living and Non-Living Things: Meaning, Examples, Characteristics and Identification of Living and Non Living Things Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 2 Basic Science and Technology
topics.content:
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
FIRST TERM
WEEK 2
PRIMARY 6 (BASIC 6)
THEME - LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS
PREVIOUS LESSON - First Term, Second Term and Third Term Basic Science and Technology Plan Lesson Notes and Scheme of Work for Primary 5 (Basic 5)
TOPIC - LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning, Examples, Characteristics and Identification Living Things
3. Meaning, Examples, Characteristics and Identification of Non Living Things
4. Different Between Living Things and Non Living Things
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define living things.
2. Define non-living things.
3. Give examples of living and non-living things.
4. State the characteristics of living things.
5. Identify living and non-living things in their environment.
6. Differentiate between living and non-living things.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about their environment, plants, animals, and natural resources. They have also observed different objects around them at home and in school.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by helping pupils identify and classify the things they see in their environment into living and non-living things based on their characteristics.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures of plants, animals, and objects
2. Real objects (stone, leaf, book, toy, flower, etc.)
3. Charts showing living and non-living things
4. Flash cards
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Everything around us can be grouped into living and non-living things. We see people, animals, and plants growing and carrying out different activities every day. We also see objects such as chairs, stones, books, and cars that do not grow or move on their own.
Living things have life and perform certain activities such as growing, breathing, feeding, reproducing, and responding to their surroundings. Non-living things do not have life and cannot perform these activities.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning, examples, characteristics, and identification of living and non-living things.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF LIVING THINGS
Living things are organisms that have life. They can grow, breathe, feed, move, reproduce, respond to their environment, and eventually die.
Examples of Living Things
- Human beings, Dog Cat
- Goat, Cow, Bird, Fish
- Frog, Ant, Butterfly, Mango tree
- Orange tree, Maize plant, Grass
- Flowering plants
Characteristics of Living Things
Living things:
1. Grow and develop.
2. Breathe (respire).
3. Feed to obtain energy.
4. Move from one place to another or show movement.
5. Reproduce young ones.
6. Respond to changes in their environment.
7. Remove waste products (excrete).
8. Eventually grow old and die.
Identification of Living Things
Living things can be identified because they:
1. Have life.
2. Need food and water to survive.
3. Grow bigger with time.
4. Breathe.
5. Reproduce.
6. Respond to touch, light, heat, and other changes.
7. Can become sick and eventually die.
Living things are organisms that have life and carry out life processes such as growth, breathing, feeding, movement, reproduction, response to stimuli, excretion, and death. Examples include humans, animals, birds, insects, and plants. These characteristics help us identify living things in our environment.
LESSON 2 - MEANING OF NON-LIVING THINGS
Non-living things are objects that do not have life. They cannot grow, breathe, feed, reproduce, respond to their environment, or die.
They do not carry out life processes like living things.
Examples of Non-Living Things
- Stone, Rock, Water, Air
- Soil, Sand, Chair, Table
- Book, Pencil, Car, Bicycle
- Computer, Ball, Building
Characteristics of Non-Living Things
Non-living things:
1. Do not grow.
2. Do not breathe.
3. Do not feed.
4. Do not reproduce.
5. Do not move by themselves.
6. Do not respond to changes in their environment.
7. Do not excrete waste.
8. Do not die because they have no life.
Identification of Non-Living Things
Non-living things can be identified because they:
1. Have no life.
2. Cannot grow or develop.
3. Do not need food or water.
4. Cannot breathe.
5. Cannot reproduce.
6. Cannot move on their own.
7. Do not respond to stimuli such as light, heat, or touch.
8. Cannot become sick or die.
Non-living things are objects that do not have life and do not perform life processes. Examples include stones, water, air, soil, books, chairs, vehicles, and buildings. They can be identified because they do not grow, breathe, feed, reproduce, move on their own, respond to stimuli, excrete waste, or die.
LESSON 3 - DIFFERENCE BETWEEN LIVING AND NON-LIVING THINGS
1. Living things have life, while non-living things do not have life.
2. Living things grow and develop, while non-living things do not grow.
3. Living things breathe (respire), while non-living things do not breathe.
4. Living things need food and water to survive, while non-living things do not need food or water.
5. Living things move on their own or show movement, while non-living things cannot move by themselves.
6. Living things reproduce young ones, while non-living things cannot reproduce.
7. Living things respond to changes in their environment (stimuli), while non-living things do not respond to stimuli.
8. Living things remove waste products from their bodies, while non-living things do not excrete waste.
9. Living things grow old and eventually die, while non-living things do not die because they have no life.
10. Examples of living things include humans, animals, birds, fish, insects, and plants, while examples of non-living things include stones, water, air, books, chairs, vehicles, and buildings.
Living things have life and perform life processes such as growing, breathing, feeding, moving, reproducing, responding to stimuli, excreting waste, and dying. Non-living things do not have life and cannot perform any of these life processes.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Objective Questions (Choose the Correct Answer)
1. Which of the following is a living thing?
A. Stone
B. Goat
C. Chair
D. Book
2. Living things can ______.
A. Grow
B. Remain the same forever
C. Never breathe
D. Never reproduce
3. Which of the following is a non-living thing?
A. Fish
B. Mango tree
C. Rock
D. Bird
4. Which of these is a characteristic of living things?
A. They do not breathe.
B. They reproduce.
C. They do not grow.
D. They cannot move.
5. Which of the following is NOT a living thing?
A. Dog
B. Butterfly
C. Car
D. Maize plant
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. Living things have ______.
7. The process by which living things produce young ones is called ______.
8. A chair is a ______ thing.
9. Plants and animals are examples of ______ things.
10. Living things respond to ______ in their environment.
C. True or False
11. Human beings are living things. ______
12. Stones can grow. ______
13. Birds breathe. ______
14. Water is a living thing. ______
15. Living things eventually die. ______
D. Short Answer Questions
16. What are living things?
17. What are non-living things?
18. Mention three examples of living things.
19. Mention three examples of non-living things.
20. State four characteristics of living things.
ANSWER GUIDE
1. B
2. A
3. C
4. B
5. C
16. Life
17. Reproduction
18. Non-living
19. Living
10. Changes (or Stimuli)
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. False
15. True
16. Living things are organisms that have life and perform life processes.
17. Non-living things are objects that do not have life and cannot perform life processes.
18. Human being, goat, bird, fish, tree, cat (any three).
19. Stone, chair, book, water, air, car (any three).
20. They grow, breathe, feed, move, reproduce, respond to stimuli, excrete waste, and die (any four).
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that living things are organisms that have life and perform life processes such as growing, breathing, feeding, moving, reproducing, responding to stimuli, excreting waste, and eventually dying.
They also learned that non-living things are objects that do not have life and cannot perform any life processes.
Pupils identified examples of living things, including humans, animals, birds, fish, insects, and plants, and examples of non-living things, such as stones, water, air, soil, books, chairs, vehicles, and buildings.
Furthermore, pupils learned the characteristics of living things, which include growth, respiration, feeding, movement, reproduction, response to stimuli, excretion, and death. They also learned that non-living things do not possess these characteristics.
Finally, pupils differentiated between living and non-living things based on their characteristics and learned how to identify them correctly in their environment.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays pictures and real objects of living and non-living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and identify the objects.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of living things in their environment.
3. The teacher explains the meaning of non-living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify examples of non-living things around them.
4. The teacher discusses the characteristics of living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the life processes performed by living things.
5. The teacher explains the characteristics of non-living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention what non-living things cannot do.
6. The teacher explains how to identify living and non-living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils classify different objects as living or non-living.
7. The teacher explains the differences between living and non-living things.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils compare the characteristics of living and non-living things.
8. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively.
9. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and take notes.
10. The teacher gives classwork and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Growing Crops: Meaning of Growing Crops, Conditions for Better Crop Growth, Types and Components of Fertilizers, Importance of Fertilizers to the Soil, and Using Fertilizer and Compost to Grow Crops Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 3 Basic Science and Technology
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What are living things?
2. What are non-living things?
3. Mention five examples each of living and non-living things.
4. State five characteristics of living things.
5. Differentiate between living and non-living things using five points.

topics.title: Drugs: Meaning, Types (Synthetic and Naturally Occurring Drugs) and Importance of Drugs Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 6 Basic Science and Technology
topics.content:
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
FIRST TERM
WEEK 6
PRIMARY 6 (BASIC 6)
THEME - LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS
PREVIOUS LESSON - The Human Circulatory System (The Blood Circulation): Meaning and Functions of Blood Vessels, Blood Circulation, and Differences Between Arteries, Veins and Capillaries Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 5 Basic Science and Technology
TOPIC - DRUGS
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Drugs
3. Difference Between Synthetic and Naturally Occurring Drugs
4. Importance of Drugs
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define drugs.
2. State the types of drugs.
3. Differentiate between synthetic and naturally occurring drugs.
4. Give examples of synthetic and naturally occurring drugs.
5. Explain the importance of drugs.
6. State the need for proper use of drugs.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the human body, diseases, infections, and healthy living. They know that people can become sick and need proper care to regain good health.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing drugs, the different types of drugs, and their importance in preventing, treating, and controlling diseases, thereby helping people maintain good health.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Samples or pictures of medicines
2. Charts showing different types of drugs
3. First aid box
4. Pictures of medicinal plants
5. Flash cards
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
People sometimes become sick because of infections, diseases, or injuries. When this happens, they may need medicines to help them recover. These medicines are called drugs. Some drugs are made from natural sources such as plants, while others are manufactured in laboratories and factories.
Drugs should always be used correctly and only under the guidance of qualified health professionals because improper use can be harmful.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of drugs, the two main types of drugs, examples of each type, and the importance of drugs in maintaining good health.
MEANING OF DRUGS
Drugs are substances used to prevent, treat, control, or cure diseases and illnesses. They help people maintain good health when used correctly and under the guidance of qualified health professionals.
Drugs should only be taken according to the instructions of a doctor, nurse, pharmacist, or other qualified healthcare provider.
Examples of Drugs
Some common examples of drugs include:
- Paracetamol - used to relieve pain and reduce fever.
- Amoxicillin - an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections.
- Ibuprofen - used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation.
- Artemether/Lumefantrine - used to treat malaria.
- Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) - used to prevent and treat dehydration caused by diarrhoea.
- Herbal medicines prepared from medicinal plants, such as ginger, neem, or aloe vera, when used appropriately.
Drugs are substances used to prevent, treat, control, or cure diseases. Examples include Paracetamol, Amoxicillin, Ibuprofen, Artemether/Lumefantrine, Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS), and some herbal medicines. Drugs are beneficial when used correctly and should always be taken according to the advice of qualified health professionals.
TYPES OF DRUGS
There are two main types of drugs:
1. Naturally Occurring Drugs
Naturally occurring drugs are obtained from natural sources such as plants, animals, and minerals. They are commonly called herbal or natural medicines.
Examples of Naturally Occurring Drugs:
- Ginger
- Garlic
- Neem leaves
- Aloe vera
- Bitter leaf
- Clove
2. Synthetic Drugs
Synthetic drugs are medicines manufactured in laboratories and pharmaceutical factories using chemicals.
Examples of Synthetic Drugs:
- Paracetamol
- Amoxicillin
- Ibuprofen
- Artemether/Lumefantrine (anti-malaria medicine)
- Cough syrup
- Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS)
DIFFERENCE BETWEEN NATURALLY OCCURRING AND SYNTHETIC DRUGS
1. Naturally occurring drugs come from natural sources, while synthetic drugs are manufactured in laboratories and factories.
2. Naturally occurring drugs are often prepared from plants, animals, or minerals, while synthetic drugs are produced using chemical processes.
3. Both types of drugs are used to prevent, treat, or control diseases when used correctly.
The two main types of drugs are naturally occurring drugs and synthetic drugs. Naturally occurring drugs come from natural sources such as plants, while synthetic drugs are produced in laboratories and factories. Both are important in treating diseases and maintaining good health when used properly.
IMPORTANCE OF DRUGS IN MAINTAINING GOOD HEALTH
Drugs are important because they help people stay healthy and recover from illnesses when used correctly.
Importance of Drugs
1. They help treat diseases and infections.
2. They relieve pain and discomfort.
3. They reduce fever.
4. They help prevent certain diseases through vaccination and other preventive medicines.
5. They help people recover more quickly from illness.
6. They control long-term health conditions such as asthma and diabetes.
7. They improve the quality of life of sick people.
8. They help save lives during serious illnesses and emergencies.
9. They promote healthy growth and development by treating illnesses promptly.
10. They help people remain active and productive.
PROPER USE OF DRUGS
To maintain good health, drugs should be used responsibly by:
1. Taking drugs only when prescribed or recommended by a qualified health professional.
2. Following the correct dosage and instructions.
3. Avoiding self-medication.
4. Checking the expiry date before using any drug.
5. Keeping drugs out of the reach of children.
6. Storing drugs according to the instructions on the label.
Drugs are important because they prevent, treat, and control diseases, relieve pain, reduce fever, save lives, and help people maintain good health. However, drugs should always be used correctly and responsibly under the guidance of qualified health professionals.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT

A. create
B. prevent and treat

D. ignore

B. Sand
C. Water
D. Salt
5. Drugs should be used ______.
A. carelessly
B. wrongly
C. responsibly
D. anyhow
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. Drugs are used to treat ______.
7. ______ drugs come from plants and animals.
8. Paracetamol is an example of a ______ drug.
9. Ginger is a ______ occurring drug.
10. Drugs should be taken according to ______ instructions.
C. True or False

12. All drugs are made in laboratories. ______
13. Aloe vera is a natural drug. ______
14. Drugs should be used without a doctor’s advice. ______
15. Drugs help maintain good health. ______
D. Short Answer Questions

17. Mention two types of drugs.
18. Give three examples of naturally occurring drugs.
19. Give three examples of synthetic drugs.
20. State three importance of drugs.
ANSWER GUIDE

2. D
3. D

5. C

20. They treat diseases, relieve pain, reduce fever, prevent diseases, and save lives (any three).
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that drugs are substances used to prevent, treat, control, or cure diseases and illnesses. Drugs help people maintain good health when used correctly.
They also learned the two main types of drugs, which are:
- Naturally occurring drugs - obtained from natural sources such as plants and animals (e.g., ginger, garlic, neem, aloe vera).
- Synthetic drugs - manufactured in laboratories and pharmaceutical factories (e.g., paracetamol, ibuprofen, amoxicillin, ORS, and malaria drugs).
Furthermore, pupils learned the importance of drugs, which include treating diseases, relieving pain, reducing fever, preventing illnesses, helping recovery, and saving lives.
Finally, pupils were taught that drugs must be used correctly and responsibly, following medical advice to avoid misuse and health risks.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher shows pictures or samples of different drugs and medicines.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and identify the materials shown.

topics.title: Drugs: Meaning and Examples of Drug Abuse, Hard Drugs and Commonly Abused Drugs, and Effects of Drug Abuse on Individuals and Society Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 8 Basic Science and Technology
topics.content:
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
FIRST TERM
WEEK 8
PRIMARY 6 (BASIC 6)
THEME - LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Drugs: Meaning, Types (Synthetic and Naturally Occurring Drugs) and Importance of Drugs Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 6 Basic Science and Technology
TOPIC - DRUG ABUSE
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Examples of Drug Abuse
3. Hard Drugs and Commonly Abused Drugs
4. Effects of Drug Abuse on Individuals and Society
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define drug abuse.
2. Give examples of drug abuse.
3. Identify commonly abused drugs.
4. State the effects of drug abuse on individuals.
5. Explain the effects of drug abuse on society.
6. State ways of avoiding drug abuse.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about drugs, the types ofdrugs (synthetic and naturally occurring), and the importance of drugs in maintaining good health.They know that drugs are useful when taken correctly under the guidance of qualified health professionals.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils that misusing drugs or taking them without proper medical advice is called drug abuse, and that drug abuse has harmful effects on individuals, families, and society.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Charts showing the dangers of drug abuse
2. Pictures of medicines and warning signs
3. Flash cards
4. Posters on healthy living
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Drugs are important for treating illnesses and keeping people healthy when they are used correctly. However, when drugs are taken without medical advice, in the wrong amount, or for the wrong purpose, they can become dangerous.
Some people misuse medicines or other harmful substances because of peer pressure, curiosity, or bad influence. This behaviour is called drug abuse.Drug abuse can affect a person’s health, education, family, and the entire society.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of drug abuse, examples of drug abuse, commonly abused drugs, and the harmful effects of drug abuse on individuals and society.
MEANING OF DRUG ABUSE
Drug abuse is the wrong or excessive use of drugs or other harmful substances in a way that is not recommended by a qualified health professional. It also includes taking drugs without a doctor’s prescription or using them for the wrong purpose.
Drug abuse can damage a person’s health and affect their behaviour, education, and future.
Examples of Drug Abuse
- Taking medicines without a doctor’s prescription.
- Taking a larger dose of medicine than prescribed.
- Using another person’s medicine without medical advice.
- Taking medicine after its expiry date.
- Using medicines for purposes other than treating illness.
- Taking drugs because of peer pressure or to feel “high.”
- Mixing different drugs without the advice of a health professional.
- Taking medicines more frequently than prescribed.
MEANING OF HARD DRUGS
Hard drugs are powerful drugs that are very dangerous and can cause serious harm to the body and brain when used without medical supervision. They can easily lead to addiction (dependence) and may damage a person’s health, behaviour, and future.
COMMONLY ABUSED DRUGS
Commonly abused drugs are substances that some people use improperly or without medical advice. Their misuse can be harmful to health.
Examples include:
- Alcohol
- Cigarettes (tobacco)
- Cough syrups used without a doctor’s prescription
- Pain-relieving medicines taken in excessive amounts
- Sleeping tablets used without medical advice
- Tranquilizers or sedative medicines used without prescription
- Cannabis (marijuana)
- Cocaine
- Heroin
- Inhalants such as glue, petrol, or paint thinner fumes
- Methamphetamine (Meth)
- Crack cocaine
- Opium
- Fentanyl (when used illegally or without medical supervision)
DANGERS OF HARD DRUGS
1. They can cause addiction.
2. They damage the brain and other body organs.
3. They affect learning and memory.
4. They may cause mental illness.
5. They can lead to crime and violence.
6. They may destroy family relationships.
7. They can result in serious illness or death.
WHY THESE DRUGS ARE ABUSED
Some people abuse drugs because of:
1. Peer pressure.
2. Curiosity.
3. Bad influence from friends.
4. Lack of proper knowledge about drugs.
5. Poor parental supervision.
6. Desire to imitate others.
7. Desire to feel excited or “high”
EFFECTS OF DRUG ABUSE ON INDIVIDUALS AND SOCIETY
Drug abuse has harmful effects on both the individual and the society.
Effects of Drug Abuse on Individuals
1. It causes poor health and damage to body organs.
2. It affects the brain, making it difficult to think clearly.
3. It leads to poor academic performance.
4. It can cause addiction (dependence on drugs).
5. It may lead to mental health problems.
6. It causes loss of self-control and irresponsible behaviour.
7. It increases the risk of accidents and injuries.
8. It may result in premature death.
Effects of Drug Abuse on Society
1. It increases crime and violence.
2. It causes insecurity in communities.
3. It leads to family problems and broken homes.
4. It reduces productivity in schools and workplaces.
5. It increases the cost of healthcare and rehabilitation.
6. It contributes to poverty and unemployment.
7. It brings shame and bad reputation to families and communities.
8. It slows the social and economic development of the nation.
HOW TO AVOID HARD DRUGS
1. Say no to drugs offered by friends or strangers.
2. Keep good friends who encourage positive behaviour.
3. Take only medicines prescribed by qualified health professionals.
4. Participate in healthy activities such as sports and reading.
5. Seek advice from parents, teachers, or counsellors when under pressure to use drugs.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS
A. Objective Questions (Choose the Correct Answer)
1. Drug abuse means __________.
A. using drugs correctly
B. the improper use of drugs
C. selling medicines
D. buying drugs
2. Which of the following is commonly abused?
A. Alcohol
B. Water
C. Milk
D. Rice
3. Which of the following is a hard drug?
A. Heroin
B. Bread
C. Orange
D. Beans
4. Drug abuse can lead to __________.
A. good health only
B. addiction
C. better eyesight
D. faster growth
5. Drugs should be taken __________.
A. without advice
B. according to medical instructions
C. anytime you like
D. in large quantities
B. Fill in the Blanks
6. Drug abuse is the __________ use of drugs.
7. Cigarettes contain __________.
8. Cocaine and heroin are examples of __________ drugs.
9. Drug abuse can affect a person’s __________ and behaviour.
10. We should take drugs only when prescribed by a qualified __________.
C. True or False
11. Drug abuse can damage the brain. ______
12. Hard drugs are safe for children. ______
13. Peer pressure can lead to drug abuse. ______
14. Drug abuse can increase crime in society. ______
15. Taking another person’s medicine without medical advice is drug abuse. ______
D. Short Answer Questions
16. What is drug abuse?
17. Mention three commonly abused drugs.
18. State three effects of drug abuse on individuals.
19. State three effects of drug abuse on society.
20. Mention three ways to prevent drug abuse.
ANSWER GUIDE
1. B
2. A
3. A
4. B
5. B
6. Improper (or wrong)
7. Nicotine
8. Hard
9. Health
10. Health professional (doctor, nurse, or pharmacist)
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. True
15. True
16. Drug abuse is the improper or excessive use of drugs without proper medical advice.
17. Alcohol, cigarettes, cough syrups, cannabis, cocaine, heroin (any three).
18. Addiction, poor health, poor academic performance, mental illness, loss of self-control (any three).
19. Crime, insecurity, family problems, poverty, reduced productivity, poor national development (any three).
20. Take drugs only as prescribed, avoid bad friends, resist peer pressure, learn about the dangers of drug abuse, seek guidance from parents, teachers, or health professionals (any three).
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that drug abuse is the improper or excessive use of drugs or medicines in a way that is not recommended by a qualified health professional. It includes taking drugs without a prescription, taking the wrong dosage, or using drugs for the wrong purpose.
They also learned examples of drug abuse, such as taking medicines without medical advice, using another person’s medicine, taking expired drugs, and taking drugs because of peer pressure.
Pupils identified some commonly abused drugs, including alcohol, cigarettes (tobacco), cough syrups, pain-relieving medicines, sleeping tablets, cannabis (marijuana), cocaine, heroin, and other hard drugs.
Furthermore, pupils learned that hard drugs are very dangerous substances that can cause addiction, serious health problems, mental illness, and even death.
Finally, pupils learned the effects of drug abuse on individuals and society. Drug abuse can damage health, affect learning, cause addiction, increase crime, lead to family problems, reduce productivity, and hinder national development. They also learned that drug abuse can be prevented by using drugs responsibly, avoiding bad company, resisting peer pressure, and following the advice of qualified health professionals.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays pictures or charts showing medicines, harmful drugs, and warning signs against drug abuse.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and identify the materials.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of drug abuse.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define drug abuse in their own words.
3. The teacher discusses examples of drug abuse.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention examples of drug abuse.
4. The teacher explains commonly abused drugs and hard drugs.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify commonly abused drugs and explain why they are dangerous.
5. The teacher discusses the causes of drug abuse.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state some causes of drug abuse, such as peer pressure and curiosity.
6. The teacher explains the effects of drug abuse on individuals.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention the harmful effects of drug abuse on health and behaviour.
7. The teacher explains the effects of drug abuse on society and discusses ways to prevent drug abuse.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the effects of drug abuse on society and suggest ways to avoid drug abuse.
8. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively.
9. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and take notes.
10. The teacher gives classwork and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

topics.title: Respiratory System: Meaning, Functions, Organs of the Respiratory System and Their Functions Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 11 Basic Science and Technology
topics.content:
BASIC SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY
FIRST TERM
WEEK 11
PRIMARY 6 (BASIC 6)
THEME - LIVING AND NON LIVING THINGS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Puberty: Meaning of Puberty, Physical and Emotional Changes, Changes in Males and Females, and Importance of Puberty in Child Development Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 10 Basic Science and Technology
TOPIC - RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Functions of Respiratory System
3. Organs That Make Up the Respiratory System and the Functions of Each Organ
4. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answer/Assignment
5. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Define the respiratory system.
2. State the functions of the respiratory system.
3. Identify the major organs of the respiratory system.
4. Explain the functions of each organ of the respiratory system.
5. Explain the importance of the respiratory system in maintaining life.
6. State ways of keeping the respiratory system healthy.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the circulatory system, the human heart, and blood circulation. They know that blood carries oxygen and nutrients to all parts of the body.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing the respiratory system, which supplies oxygen to the body through breathing and removes carbon dioxide. Pupils will also learn about the major organs of the respiratory system and the functions of each organ.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Chart of the human respiratory system
2. Diagram showing the lungs and air passages
3. Model of the respiratory system
4. Flash cards
5. Textbooks
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every living person needs oxygen to stay alive. We obtain oxygen by breathing through a special body system known as the respiratory system. This system is made up of organs that work together to take in oxygen from the air and remove carbon dioxide from the body.
Without the respiratory system, the body cannot get the oxygen needed to produce energy and keep body organs functioning properly.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of the respiratory system, its functions, the organs that make up the respiratory system, and the functions of each organ.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
The respiratory system is the body system responsible for breathing. It takes in oxygen from the air and removes carbon dioxide from the body.
The respiratory system works together with the circulatory system to supply oxygen to all body cells and remove waste gases.
FUNCTIONS OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
1. It takes in oxygen from the air during breathing.
2. It removes carbon dioxide from the body during exhalation.
3. It supplies oxygen needed by body cells to produce energy.
4. It helps keep the body alive by supporting all body organs.
5. It filters dust, germs, and other harmful particles from the air before they reach the lungs.
6. It helps in speaking by allowing air to pass through the voice box.
7. It helps maintain a healthy balance of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the body.
LESSON 2 - IMPORTANCE OF THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
1. It provides oxygen needed for life.
2. It removes harmful waste gases from the body.
3. It supports the production of energy in body cells.
4. It works with the circulatory system to keep the body healthy.
5. It enables normal breathing and speaking.
CARING FOR THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM
1. Avoid smoking and second-hand smoke.
2. Breathe clean, fresh air whenever possible.
3. Exercise regularly.
4. Keep the environment clean and free from dust.
5. Cover your nose and mouth when coughing or sneezing.
6. Seek medical attention when experiencing breathing difficulties.
LESSON 3 - ORGANS THAT MAKE UP THE RESPIRATORY SYSTEM AND THE FUNCTIONS OF EACH ORGAN
The respiratory system is made up of several organs that work together to help us breathe:
1. Nose (Nostrils)
Functions:
- It allows air to enter the body.
- It filters dust and germs from the air.
- It warms and moistens the air before it reaches the lungs.
2. Pharynx (Throat)
Functions:
- It serves as a passage for air from the nose to the larynx.
- It helps move air into the respiratory system.
3. Larynx (Voice Box)
Functions:
- It allows air to pass into the trachea.
- It produces sound for speaking.
- It protects the airway during swallowing.
4. Trachea (Windpipe)
Functions:
- It carries air from the larynx to the lungs.
- It helps filter dust and other particles before the air reaches the lungs.
5. Bronchi
Functions:
- They are tubes that carry air from the trachea into the right and left lungs.
- They distribute air throughout the lungs.
6. Lungs
Functions:
- The are the main organs of breathing.
- They absorb oxygen into the blood.
- They remove carbon dioxide from the blood.
7. Diaphragm
Functions:
- It is a sstrong muscle below the lungs.
- It helps the lungs expand during inhalation.
- It helps push air out of the lungs during exhalation.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Objective Questions (Choose the Correct Answer)
1. The respiratory system is responsible for ______.
A. digestion
B. breathing
C. circulation
D. movement

C. True or False

D. Short Answer Questions

17. Mention four organs of the respiratory system.
18. State three functions of the respiratory system.
19. What is the function of the lungs?
20. Mention three ways of keeping the respiratory system healthy.
ANSWER GUIDE
1. B
2. C
3. A
4. D
5. A
6. Carbon dioxide
7. Nose (or nostrils)
8. Bronchi
9. Larynx (voice box)
10. Oxygen

12. False
13. True
14. True
15. False
16. The respiratory system is the body system responsible for breathing. It takes in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
17. Nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, diaphragm (any four).
18. It takes in oxygen, removes carbon dioxide, helps body cells produce energy, filters air, and helps in speaking (any three).
19. The lungs absorb oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide from the blood.
20. Breathe clean air, avoid smoking and second-hand smoke, exercise regularly, keep the environment clean, and seek medical care for breathing problems (any three).
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that the respiratory system is the body system responsible for breathing. It takes in oxygen from the air and removes carbon dioxide from the body.
They also learned the functions of the respiratory system, which include supplying oxygen to the body, removing carbon dioxide, helping body cells produce energy, supporting life, filtering harmful particles from the air, and assisting in speaking.
Furthermore, pupils identified the major organs of the respiratory system, namely:
- Nose (Nostrils)
- Pharynx (Throat)
- Larynx (Voice Box)
- Trachea (Windpipe)
- Bronchi
- Lungs
- Diaphragm
They learned the functions of each organ and how they work together to make breathing possible.
Finally, pupils learned the importance of keeping the respiratory system healthy by breathing clean air, avoiding smoking and second-hand smoke, exercising regularly, maintaining good personal hygiene, and seeking medical attention when experiencing breathing difficulties.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. The teacher displays a chart or model of the human respiratory system.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the chart and identify the organs shown.
2. The teacher explains the meaning of the respiratory system.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils define the respiratory system in their own words.
3. The teacher discusses the functions of the respiratory system.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the functions of the respiratory system.
4. The teacher identifies the major organs of the respiratory system on the chart.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and name the organs of the respiratory system.
5. The teacher explains the function of each organ of the respiratory system.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state the functions of the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, and diaphragm.
6. The teacher demonstrates the process of breathing (inhalation and exhalation).
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe and practise breathing in and breathing out correctly.
7. The teacher discusses the importance of keeping the respiratory system healthy.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention healthy habits that protect the respiratory system.
8. The teacher asks oral questions based on the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and participate actively.
9. The teacher summarizes the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils participate in the summary and take notes.
10. The teacher gives classwork and provides corrections where necessary.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the exercise and correct their mistakes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.

Air: Meaning, Properties, Applications of Air, Meaning and the Uses (Importance) of Air Pressure Primary 5 (Basic 5) Second Term Week 2 Basic Science and Technology
LESSON EVALUATION
